title: How Buffett measures float, look-through earnings and margin of safety: 1990 letter
summary: Buffett's 1990 letter explains look-through earnings, judging insurance by cost of float, why falling stock prices help permanent buyers, why debt-funded junk bonds fail, and what kind of business Berkshire wants to buy. It also covers managers over industry economics and bank leverage.

principles.text: Accounting earnings are a starting point; what matters is who owns retained earnings and how they are used.
principles.quote: We care not whether the auditors hear a tree fall in the forest; we do care who owns the tree and what's next done with it.

principles.text: Judge insurers by underwriting loss relative to float: a low cost of funds means a good business.
principles.quote: A low cost of funds signifies a good business; a high cost translates into a poor business.

principles.text: If you will be a lifelong buyer, welcome falling prices; optimism is the buyer's enemy.
principles.quote: It's optimism that is the enemy of the rational buyer.

principles.text: Margin of safety is the core of investing, and heavy debt violates it because business roads have potholes.
principles.quote: The roads of business are riddled with potholes; a plan that requires dodging them all is a plan for disaster.

principles.text: Superior returns come from outstanding operating managers, not just good industries.
principles.quote: Our extraordinary returns flow from outstanding operating managers, not fortuitous industry economics.

principles.text: Prefer lumpy higher returns to smooth lower ones; volatility is fine if long-term results are superior.
principles.quote: Charlie and I always have preferred a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%.
